content.text:
This PostgreSQL 15 SELECT takes 20 seconds on a large table. How would you speed it up?

```sql
SELECT customer_id, MAX(created_at)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

payload.last_agent_message:
I’d start with the actual plan, then test a partial index. The best approach depends on how many orders are paid, how many customers there are, and whether the query is spending its time reading data or aggregating it.

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, MAX(created_at)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

Look at the scan type, estimated versus actual rows, buffer reads, and whether a sort or hash aggregate spills to disk. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the query, and its timing excludes sending the result rows to the client. [PostgreSQL EXPLAIN documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/using-explain.html)

A useful index to benchmark is:

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_paid_customer_created_idx
ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)
WHERE status = 'paid';
```

It contains only paid orders, orders entries by customer, and can allow an index-only scan. That can reduce I/O, especially when paid orders are a small fraction of the table. Index-only scans still need heap visits for pages whose visibility-map bits are not set, so check **Heap Fetches** in the plan and ensure vacuum is keeping up. The index also costs storage and adds work to writes. `CONCURRENTLY` avoids blocking ordinary writes during the build, but takes more work and cannot run inside a transaction block. [Index-only scans](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/indexes-index-only-scans.html) · [CREATE INDEX](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-createindex.html)

**The index is not guaranteed to make this fast.** PostgreSQL 15 will generally still scan the matching index entries to compute the grouped maximum; it does not automatically jump to one entry per customer for this query. If most orders are paid, a parallel sequential scan and aggregate may be faster. Refresh statistics with `ANALYZE orders` if estimates are stale, and compare plans before and after the index. [Parallel aggregation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/parallel-plans.html) · [ANALYZE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-analyze.html)

If there are **many paid orders per customer** and you already have a much smaller, complete customer list, benchmark a different shape: perform one indexed lookup per customer using a lateral subquery and `ORDER BY created_at DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 1`. That requires a matching index order and careful handling of customers with no paid orders and nullable values. For a frequently requested result where some staleness is acceptable, a materialized summary is another option; if it must be current, maintaining a summary table moves work to writes and needs to account for updates, deletions, and status changes.

Share the `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output, existing indexes, and approximate counts of paid orders and distinct customers for a more specific recommendation.
